{"id": "2:206/q02", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported for these verses?", "turns_on": "Reports locate the passage in different events or treat its class description as general.", "positions": [{"id": "2:206/q02/p1", "position": "Al-Akhnas's profession of Islam and subsequent destruction of crops and livestock.", "reasons": "Elmalılı gives his tribe, alliance, profession before the Prophet, and burning of a Muslim field and killing of animals."}, {"id": "2:206/q02/p2", "position": "The al-Raji expedition and the hypocrites' mockery of its martyrs.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak recount Quraysh's false conversion request, six Muslims lured, three killed, and Khubayb and Zayd captured; Ibn Abbas reports hypocrites calling the deaths pointless. Ibn Jawzi's report names al-Zubayr, al-Miqdad and Khubayb with the hypocrites. Tha'labi adds Khubayb's refusal of treachery and miraculous fruit in Mecca. Baghawi reports Umar marveling that God protected Asim's body from polytheists after death, in keeping with Asim's vow not to touch or be touched by one."}, {"id": "2:206/q02/p3", "position": "Suhayb's escape after giving up his wealth to reach Medina.", "reasons": "Nasafi reports polytheists attempting to make him leave Islam, killing companions with him, then allowing him to travel after taking his wealth."}, {"id": "2:206/q02/p4", "position": "One who enjoins right and forbids wrong until killed.", "reasons": "Nasafi also reports this possible occasion or application."}, {"id": "2:206/q02/p5", "position": "Hypocrites generally, with no exclusive individual occasion.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan reports identify hypocrites; Kur'an Yolu reports they appeared friendly before the Prophet while acting destructively in secret. Study Quran says most cited commentators prefer a universal teaching despite incident reports."}]}

{"id": "2:206/q04", "question": "What does the call to fear God ask him to do?", "turns_on": "How broadly the unstated object of 'fear' and the surrounding faults are supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "2:206/q04/p1", "position": "Revere God and guard against His punishment and disobedience.", "reasons": "Tabrisi derives ittiqa' from taking protection against danger; al-Asamm includes fearing punishment and avoiding disobedience. {"id": "2:206/q07", "question": "What does ٱلْعِزَّةُ mean here?", "turns_on": "The word's base sense of strength versus its contextual sense as zeal or claimed status.", "positions": [{"id": "2:206/q07/p1", "position": "Strength, might, protection or invulnerability, turned into haughtiness in context.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabrisi define strength warding off humiliation; Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur add force, tribal backing or confidence that no one may challenge him. Biqa'i recalls 10:65 to say all true might belongs to God."}, {"id": "2:206/q07/p2", "position": "Partisan, jāhiliyya zeal and proud obstinacy.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tustari compare 38:2; Ibn Abbas is reported glossing it as zealotry with a cited poem; Ibn Jawzi's third Quranic use cites 38:2. {"id": "2:228/q07", "question": "How are 'three qurūʾ' construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the numeral is a temporal accusative or the verb's direct object.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q07/p1", "position": "An accusative duration: they wait a time of three cycles.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi parse it as duration, often supplying an omitted object such as marriage or the passage of time."}, {"id": "2:228/q07/p2", "position": "A direct object: they wait for three cycles to pass.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Samin also report this parse; Nahhas paraphrases with counting their waiting period."}]}

{"id": "2:228/q22", "question": "What does 'more entitled' compare or imply?", "turns_on": "Whether it expresses priority over a rival or is a noncomparative intensive.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q22/p1", "position": "The first husband has priority over other suitors or over her postwaiting freedom.", "reasons": "Razi and Qurtubi explain that her control of herself begins after the waiting period; Tabataba'i compares other suitors; Kuranyolu cites family ties and shared history."}, {"id": "2:228/q22/p2", "position": "It means simply entitled, since no rival can revoke during the term.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin, Bursevi and Alusi treat the comparative as emphasis: another suitor has no revocation right and she cannot veto a valid return."}, {"id": "2:228/q22/p3", "position": "It can mean revocation is more beloved to God than divorce.", "reasons": "Alusi records this gloss and the report calling divorce the most detested lawful act."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q23", "question": "What counts as revocation during the waiting period?", "turns_on": "Whether words, intercourse or other intimate acts suffice, with or without intent and witnesses.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q23/p1", "position": "A spoken declaration alone is required.", "reasons": "Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, Jabir ibn Zayd and Abu Qilaba require speech; some additionally require witnesses. Intercourse before words is treated as unlawful, and Shafi'i assigns equivalent dower."}, {"id": "2:228/q23/p2", "position": "Intercourse or lustful acts themselves effect revocation, regardless of intent.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa, Thawri, al-Layth and some Malikis count intercourse; Hanafis add desire-based touching or looking. Witnesses are recommended by many."}, {"id": "2:228/q23/p3", "position": "Intercourse or intimate acts count if the husband intended return.", "reasons": "Malik and Ishaq require intent for intercourse; some Malikis include kissing and touch. They urge witnesses, but the return may take effect without them."}, {"id": "2:228/q23/p4", "position": "Revocation requires ordinary new-marriage safeguards unless independent proof removes them.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan questions a unilateral return without contract conditions because divorce separates the spouses, while acknowledging the jurists' common contrary rule."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q24", "question": "Is intercourse permitted with a revocably divorced wife before revocation?", "turns_on": "Whether revocable divorce removes present sexual permissibility or only sets a course toward separation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q24/p1", "position": "No; divorce suspends intimacy and return restores permission literally.", "reasons": "Malik, Shafi'i and Qurtubi's school prohibit intimacy and travel together until return; Qurtubi prefers literal 'return' and cites the lost permission."}, {"id": "2:228/q24/p2", "position": "Yes; marriage rulings remain and return figuratively reverses impending separation.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa and al-Layth say divorce reduces the remaining count but current marriage remains; Nasafi and Bursevi cite calling them husbands."}, {"id": "2:228/q24/p3", "position": "Conduct such as seclusion, adornment, entry and travel is regulated differently by schools.", "reasons": "Malik restricts private access; Abu Hanifa allows seeing and adornment; Shafi'i treats her like an irrevocably divorced woman until spoken revocation. Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan transmit the detailed disagreements."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q25", "question": "To what does 'during that' refer?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative points to the waiting period, concealed pregnancy, or restored marriage.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q25/p1", "position": "The waiting period of cycles, months or pregnancy.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Qatada, Tabari, Zajjaj, Baydawi and others say the right lasts until the term ends; Samin and Alusi discuss attachment to 'entitled' or 'return'."}, {"id": "2:228/q25/p2", "position": "The concealed pregnancy or the marriage being restored.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports pregnancy as another antecedent; Abu al-Baqa' takes the demonstrative as marriage."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q26", "question": "What does intending reconciliation require?", "turns_on": "Whether good intent conditions legal effect or concerns moral permission alone.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q26/p1", "position": "The husband should repair the estrangement and not prolong distress.", "reasons": "Tabari, Wahidi, Qushayri, Mawrdi and others cite the abusive practice of returning near the end of a term only to divorce again; 2:231 warns against harm."}, {"id": "2:228/q26/p2", "position": "A harmful return is sinful but legally effective.", "reasons": "Tabari, Jishumi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Alusi and others distinguish inward intent from outward effect; Ibn al-Jawzi reasons 2:231 would not threaten an invalid act."}, {"id": "2:228/q26/p3", "position": "Without sincere reform, return is inwardly illicit.", "reasons": "Biqa'i calls such a hidden motive inwardly adulterous, while leaving outward legal judgment to God."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q27", "question": "What reciprocal rights do spouses have?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause especially bars mutual harm, exemplifies duties, or states a general principle of all marital rights.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q27/p1", "position": "Each owes enforceable good treatment, though their duties need not be identical.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Zajjaj, Baydawi, Nasafi, Tabarsi and later writers include maintenance, clothing, companionship, fidelity, obedience and freedom from harm; Prophetic reports forbid striking the face or insulting a wife."}, {"id": "2:228/q27/p2", "position": "Mutual adornment and attention to sexual needs are applications.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas adorns himself for his wife as she does for him; Qurtubi and others include fitting grooming and her sexual satisfaction."}, {"id": "2:228/q27/p3", "position": "In context the specific reciprocal duty is to avoid harming one another.", "reasons": "Tabari prefers it because husbands must not revoke to hurt and wives must not conceal pregnancy or blood to hurt."}, {"id": "2:228/q27/p4", "position": "The statement embraces every marital right and establishes women's standing.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Ashur, Tabataba'i and Kuranyolu stress its breadth. Ibn Ashur says women's rights are named first because custom long ignored them; later authors discuss women's independent property and agency."}]}
